intro: Varese is the garden city of Lombardy, at the foot of the Alps between Lake Maggiore and Lake Como, its villas and parks full of trees planted in the nineteenth century. A reader sent us two that Italy's national register of monumental trees also lists: a vast Lebanon cedar 34 metres tall and a ginkgo 365 centimetres round that turns gold in November.
meta_description: Varese's monumental trees: a vast cedar of Lebanon and a ginkgo that turns gold in November, both on Italy's national register.
question_meta: Varese's monumental trees: a vast cedar of Lebanon and a ginkgo that turns gold in November, both on Italy's national register.
question_answer: The cedar and the ginkgo stand a few dozen metres apart in a public garden off Viale Sant'Antonio in Varese. Both are free to see.
question_context: Varese calls itself the garden city, and its villas and public parks hold some of the finest planted trees in Lombardy, many of them set out in the nineteenth century when exotic conifers and Asian trees were the fashion. Italy's national register of monumental trees, kept by the agriculture ministry, lists a number of them. A reader sent us two that stand a few dozen metres apart in a public garden off Viale Sant'Antonio, and both match register entries. The first is a cedar of Lebanon, recorded at 34 metres tall, whose several trunks carry a dark, tiered crown so broad it fills the photograph, with benches and information boards set out in front of it like seats before a stage. The second is a ginkgo, recorded at 365 centimetres round and 28 metres tall, which the reader photographed from below in November with every leaf turned butter yellow. Ginkgo is a living fossil, almost unchanged for some two hundred million years, and reached Europe from Asian temple gardens in the eighteenth century. We do not know when either tree was planted. The garden's boards may say, and if they do, tell us on the trees' pages.

faq.q: What are the monumental trees of Varese?
faq.a: A cedar of Lebanon 34 metres tall and a ginkgo 365 centimetres round, both listed on Italy's national register of monumental trees, standing in the same garden.

faq.q: When is the ginkgo at its best?
faq.a: In mid-November, when its leaves turn butter yellow all at once, shortly before they fall.
Yes, they stand in a public garden.

trees.story:
Italy keeps a national register of its monumental trees, and Varese, the garden city at the foot of the Alps between Lake Maggiore and Lake Como, has several. A reader sent us this one, and the register lists a Lebanon cedar here, 34 metres tall.

The photograph shows a tree that has outgrown its garden. Several trunks rise together from the lawn and carry a dark, tiered crown so broad that it fills the frame from side to side, the layered branches stepping out in the flat shelves that make a cedar of Lebanon recognisable from far away. At its foot a low fence keeps people off the roots, and in front of it the garden has set out benches, information boards and a white bench painted with a red heart, all facing the tree as if it were a stage.

Cedars of Lebanon came to Italy's gardens from the mountains of the eastern Mediterranean, and in the parks of Lombardy's villas some of the first plantings have grown into giants like this one. We do not know when this one was planted; the boards in front of it may say, and if they do, tell us here.

Sit on the heart bench and look up.

trees.story:
A few dozen metres from the great cedar of the same garden in Varese stands a ginkgo that Italy's national register of monumental trees also lists: 365 centimetres round and 28 metres tall. The same reader sent us both, in November, when this one was at its best.

In one sense ginkgo is the oldest tree on the planet, since the species has barely changed in some two hundred million years and was found by Europeans only in the temple gardens of China and Japan, from where it reached Europe in the eighteenth century. Planted in Italian parks, it became a favourite for exactly what the reader photographed, a few weeks each autumn when every fan-shaped leaf turns butter yellow at once.

The photograph looks straight up the trunk. It is thick, dark and ridged, and it opens into long limbs that reach out level in every direction, each one hung with gold against a hard blue sky. Soon after, a ginkgo drops nearly all its leaves within a few days, carpeting the ground.

"It was planted in 1865, in Mirabello villa's garden," the reader who sent it tells us, "near to the cedar of Lebanon." That date is theirs; the register does not give one.

Come in mid-November and stand right under it.
